VIS104 · WEEK 05 · ANALOG DRAWING

Chance, Data, and Participation

An instruction can receive inputs the artist does not fully control. A chance event, a recorded value or another person’s contribution enters through a designed rule and leaves a visible trace.

Who or what supplies the next decision?

Reference works

01 / LECTURE

Lecture overview

  • Source, rule and traceIdentify what enters, how it becomes a mark or choice, and what the work preserves.
  • Chance and selectionAn uncertain event supplies some decisions; the artist still defines its conditions and later interventions.
  • Data and translationValues become visual form through sampling, selection and an explicit mapping.
  • Participation and authorshipPeople supply choices or marks; the invitation and combining rule determine how those contributions survive.

02 / LAB · EXECUTE A CLASSIC WORK

Arp and Chance Collage

Students perform one bounded chance procedure individually. Material choices happen before the drop; its first arrangement is recorded and preserved.

  1. Set the conditions. Prepare exactly twelve rough paper squares or rectangles and a landscape A3 support.
  2. Release once. Drop the complete set once from about 30 cm above the center. The fall determines positions, rotations and overlaps.
  3. Record the chance state. Photograph before moving anything. Keep pieces that touch or overlap the sheet; exclude pieces completely outside, without dropping them again.
  4. Preserve the arrangement. Glue according to the record, including layer relationships. Document accidents or necessary restoration rather than improving the composition.

A classroom study after Arp, not a reconstruction of his exact process. The museum record notes that chance did not necessarily remove later artistic control; this lab deliberately preserves the first drop.

StudyProcedureWhat becomes visible
Before the dropThe student fixes materials, piece count and boundary treatment.Authorship establishes the conditions.
After the dropThe first state is recorded and preserved.No preferred arrangement is selected afterwards.

03 / EXERCISE · DESIGN AN ORIGINAL WORK

Design a Composite Drawing with Participation

Each student authors a bounded drawing instruction for four people, then combines all four contributions through a preplanned transcription rule. Physical chance determines order and rotation.

  1. Write before collecting. Fix a shared prompt, four 10 × 10 cm drawing areas, a two-minute contribution, four A3 placement positions and a copying/boundary rule.
  2. Invite four contributions. Four different people each interpret the same written instruction. Keep all four originals; do not collect extras to choose favorites.
  3. Log the chance decisions. Blind-draw participant order without replacement. Draw a clockwise angle for each contribution from 0°, 90°, 180° and 270°, replacing the angle slip each time.
  4. Make the composite. Hand-copy every contribution at the same scale into its assigned position and angle. Preserve overlaps and keep the originals, rule sheet and chance log.

The lab preserves an event; the exercise designs a new system that combines other people’s marks with chance.

References for student design

These works offer ways to structure a new system. Students develop their own instruction and relationships.

Outputs

Lab
One labeled A3 collage, the first chance-state and final photographs, and a short process note.
Exercise
One A3 composite, a rule sheet and four-row chance log, all four original drawings, and concise process evidence.
